power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To our knowledge, no previous studies investigated the relationships between discussed two types of political knowledge, national identity and anti-democratic sentiments hence reliable indirect effect sizes from comparable research were unavailable. Therefore, we were unable to conduct a priori power analyses and the sample size was determined based on economic criteria. We evaluated statistical power using Monte Carlo simulations based on parameter estimates obtained in Study 1 (5,000 replications) with pwrSEM (Wang & Rhemtulla, 2021). The results indicated high power (> .99; Cohen, 1988) to detect the indirect effects under the observed model parameters.

Since we introduced a novel construct to Study 2 (Poland as a democratic state), which, to our knowledge, was not used in previous studies, we were not able to perform a priori power analyses for hypothesized serial indirect effects pathways. Therefore, we adopted a similar approach to estimating power as in Study 1. To this end, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations using parameter estimates derived from Study 2 (5,000 replications) implemented in pwrSEM (Wang & Rhemtulla, 2021). The simulations suggested that the study had high sensitivity (> .99; Cohen, 1988) to detect the hypothesized indirect effects given the specified model and parameter values. As these estimates depend on the assumed population parameters, they should be interpreted as conditional on the fitted model. Detailed results are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .06", Sentence = "Additionally, current political knowledge showed indirect effects on support for democracy (IE = -0.26, SE = 0.13, 95% CI [-0.57, -0.08], p < .05), dictatorship endorsement (IE = 0.22, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [0.07, 0.48], p < .05) and conspiracy beliefs (IE = 0.19, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.05, 0.42], p = .06) via higher national narcissism."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 132 columns across 2 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------

), Outcome = c("errored", "errored"), Detail = c("undefined_variable",

-2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**2 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
), "Missing variable" = c("data1", "data1"), "Defined in" = c("(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)",
```

#### SPSS data without syntax

An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.por`) is present but **no SPSS syntax file (`.sps`) was found**, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in **jamovi** (`.omv`) or **JASP** (`.jasp`) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

info.title: Knowing the Rules of the Game: Political Knowledge as a Buffer Against National Narcissism and Anti-Democratic Sentiment
keywords: Piotr Michalski: conceptualization, methodology, formal analysis and investigation, writingoriginal draft preparation, review and editing, data curation

text.text: We have no known conflicts of interests to disclose.
These studies were performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Approval was granted by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology, Polish Academy of Sciences (20.11.2024).

As Dahl (2020) argues, democratic systems thrive when citizens are informed about political processes and actively participate in civic life, ensuring that decisions serve the broader public good rather than narrow partisan interests.
In recent decades, scholars have documented a gradual erosion of democratic norms across many Western nations.
This decline is reflected in reduced trust in democratic institutions, the rise of populist leaders, and deepening political polarization (Hyde, 2020).
text.formatted: This decline is reflected in reduced trust in democratic institutions, the rise of populist leaders, and deepening political polarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hyde, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These developments prompt an important question: why some individuals lose faith in democracy, and through what psychological mechanisms does this occur?
We examine a central psychological construct in this study: national narcissism, also known as collective narcissism (Marchlewska et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We examine a central psychological construct in this study: national narcissism, also known as collective narcissism <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Marchlewska et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This refers to an exaggerated belief in the nation's superiority, sustained by a need for recognition from others (Golec de Zavala et al., 2009).
text.formatted: This refers to an exaggerated belief in the nation's superiority, sustained by a need for recognition from others <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Golec de Zavala et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Research has shown that individuals high in national narcissism often reject pluralistic values (Golec de Zavala & Keenan, 2023), display greater openness to conspiracy narratives (Michalski et al., 2023a), and endorse discriminatory attitudes toward marginalized groups within the nation (Szczepańska et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Research has shown that individuals high in national narcissism often reject pluralistic values <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Golec de Zavala & Keenan, 2023)</ref>, display greater openness to conspiracy narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Michalski et al., 2023a)</ref>, and endorse discriminatory attitudes toward marginalized groups within the nation <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Szczepańska et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: They may also support hierarchical arrangements that perpetuate inequality (Golec de Zavala, 2024).
text.formatted: They may also support hierarchical arrangements that perpetuate inequality <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Golec de Zavala, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such defensively oriented identities are frequently reinforced by populist rhetoric portraying the nation as morally exceptional yet constantly under threat from both internal and external sources (Marchlewska et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Such defensively oriented identities are frequently reinforced by populist rhetoric portraying the nation as morally exceptional yet constantly under threat from both internal and external sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Marchlewska et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Prior research has linked national narcissism to reduced support for democratic governance (Marchlewska et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Prior research has linked national narcissism to reduced support for democratic governance <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Marchlewska et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: More recent studies suggest that insufficient knowledge of democratic norms and institutional structures may contribute to the development of this defensive identity (Michalski et al., 2023a).
text.formatted: More recent studies suggest that insufficient knowledge of democratic norms and institutional structures may contribute to the development of this defensive identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Michalski et al., 2023a)</ref>.

text.text: We argue that individuals lacking "rules of the game" knowledge are more likely to adopt a narcissistic form of national identity.
This, in turn, can diminish democratic commitment, strengthen preferences for authoritarian leadership, and increase receptivity to conspiracy narratives.

Limited understanding of democratic principles may leave citizens vulnerable to rhetoric portraying the national ingroup as undervalued and under constant threatdiscourse that can, over time, cultivate anti-democratic attitudes.

Numerous studies have shown that political knowledge is central to sustaining democratic life, fostering civic engagement, encouraging solidarity with fellow citizens, and reducing support for autocratic or populist governance (e.g., Cho, 2014; Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996; Delli Carpini, 2005; Galston, 2001).
text.formatted: Numerous studies have shown that political knowledge is central to sustaining democratic life, fostering civic engagement, encouraging solidarity with fellow citizens, and reducing support for autocratic or populist governance (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cho, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Delli Carpini, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Galston, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Politically informed citizens are more likely to recognize threats to democratic governance, critically assess populist rhetoric, and reject oversimplified narratives that scapegoat outgroups or promote authoritarian solutions to complex problems (Galston, 2001).
text.formatted: Politically informed citizens are more likely to recognize threats to democratic governance, critically assess populist rhetoric, and reject oversimplified narratives that scapegoat outgroups or promote authoritarian solutions to complex problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Galston, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: But what exactly constitutes political knowledge, and how should we conceptualize it in the context of democratic functioning?
Studies indicate that political knowledge is not a unidimensional construct as it has different sources (Barabas et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Studies indicate that political knowledge is not a unidimensional construct as it has different sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barabas et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: One dimension, often cultivated through formal education, involves understanding the stable principles and structures of politics -what is commonly referred to as "rules of the game" knowledge.

Another, more fluid dimension, is "current political knowledge", which reflects awareness of ongoing events and political actors, acquired through engagement with news and public affairs (Michalski et al., 2023a; 2023b).
text.formatted: Another, more fluid dimension, is "current political knowledge", which reflects awareness of ongoing events and political actors, acquired through engagement with news and public affairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Michalski et al., 2023a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">2023b)</ref>.

text.text: While such awareness can produce "vigilant citizens" (Norris, 2011), it may also encourage perceptions of politics as an arena of constant conflict, potentially undermining confidence in the system's effectiveness.
text.formatted: While such awareness can produce "vigilant citizens" <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Norris, 2011)</ref>, it may also encourage perceptions of politics as an arena of constant conflict, potentially undermining confidence in the system's effectiveness.

text.text: We argue that rules of the game knowledge (encompassing democratic principles, institutional functions, and system structure) plays a particularly important role in fostering and sustaining democratic support (Cho, 2014; Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996).
text.formatted: We argue that rules of the game knowledge (encompassing democratic principles, institutional functions, and system structure) plays a particularly important role in fostering and sustaining democratic support <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cho, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Prior research shows that this form of knowledge promotes unconventional participation by clarifying how citizens can influence politics (Michalski et al., 2023b) and serves as a protective factor against national narcissism and climate change conspiracy beliefs (Michalski et al., 2023a).
text.formatted: Prior research shows that this form of knowledge promotes unconventional participation by clarifying how citizens can influence politics <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Michalski et al., 2023b)</ref> and serves as a protective factor against national narcissism and climate change conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Michalski et al., 2023a)</ref>.

text.text: In our framework, it is treated as a civic resource that equips individuals to navigate institutional complexity, interpret political processes, and act effectively within a democratic system.

Moreover, it may help inoculate citizens against populist rhetoric that reduces complex realities to emotionally charged divisions between "the people" and "the elites" as well as against other anti-democratic narratives.

Studies consistently show that citizens with a strong understanding of democratic systems (reflected in high rules of the game knowledge) tend to hold political attitudes that strengthen democratic governance.
For example, they are generally less polarized and less likely to support candidates who promote anti-democratic positions (Eroglu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, they are generally less polarized and less likely to support candidates who promote anti-democratic positions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Eroglu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: They also display greater tolerance for political diversity (e.g., Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996; Galston, 2001; Hall, 2018) and report fewer negative health effects from political stress (Smith, 2022).
text.formatted: They also display greater tolerance for political <ref type="bibr">diversity (e.g., Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Galston, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hall, 2018)</ref> and report fewer negative health effects from political stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Smith, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, individuals with substantial political knowledge are less inclined to restrict civil liberties when confronted with threats (Carriere et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Likewise, individuals with substantial political knowledge are less inclined to restrict civil liberties when confronted with threats <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Carriere et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A common thread in these findings is psychological security (Sniderman, 1975), which rules of the game knowledge can enhance in two ways: by making political processes more understandable, thereby reducing uncertainty (Galston, 2001), and by increasing political efficacy through clearer pathways for exerting influence on political decisionmakers (Michalski et al., 2023b; Reichert, 2016).
text.formatted: A common thread in these findings is psychological security <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sniderman, 1975)</ref>, which rules of the game knowledge can enhance in two ways: by making political processes more understandable, thereby reducing uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Galston, 2001)</ref>, and by increasing political efficacy through clearer pathways for exerting influence on political decisionmakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Michalski et al., 2023b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Reichert, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This security fosters respect for differing viewpoints and helps guard against authoritarian impulses (Sniderman, 1975; Marchlewska et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This security fosters respect for differing viewpoints and helps guard against authoritarian impulses <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sniderman, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Marchlewska et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, when psychological security is lacking, individuals may resist compromise, view political diversity negatively, and challenge democratic norms intended to accommodate a range of perspectives (Peffley & Rohrschneider, 2003).
text.formatted: Conversely, when psychological security is lacking, individuals may resist compromise, view political diversity negatively, and challenge democratic norms intended to accommodate a range of perspectives <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Peffley & Rohrschneider, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: When psychological security is lacking, national identification can take forms that undermine democratic support.
Research shows that the character of national identity significantly shapes citizens' commitment to democracy (Erhardt et al., 2021; Marchlewska et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Research shows that the character of national identity significantly shapes citizens' commitment to democracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Erhardt et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Marchlewska et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This connection is rooted in psychological processes, with low security, such as diminished personal control, emerging as a key factor in how individuals relate to their nation (Cichocka et al., 2018; Marchlewska et al., 2020; Cichocka & Cisłak, 2020; Golec de Zavala et al., 2019; Marchlewska et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This connection is rooted in psychological processes, with low security, such as diminished personal control, emerging as a key factor in how individuals relate to their nation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cichocka et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Marchlewska et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cichocka & Cisłak, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Golec de Zavala et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Marchlewska et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: National narcissism is understood as a defensive form of ingroup identity arising from unmet individual and collective needs (Cichocka, 2016).
text.formatted: National narcissism is understood as a defensive form of ingroup identity arising from unmet individual and collective needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cichocka, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Marchlewska et al. (2018) found that inducing perceptions of long-term disadvantage for the national ingroup raised levels of national narcissism.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Marchlewska et al. (2018)</ref> found that inducing perceptions of long-term disadvantage for the national ingroup raised levels of national narcissism.

text.text: In their study, this disadvantage was framed as the belief that outsiders had systematically diminished the nation's influence and sovereignty.
Elevated national narcissism subsequently predicted greater support for populist policies.

In situations of perceived threat, national narcissism often serves as a compensatory response, sought through the perceived grandiosity of the national group (Golec de Zavala et al., 2009; Marchlewska et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In situations of perceived threat, national narcissism often serves as a compensatory response, sought through the perceived grandiosity of the national group (Golec de <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Zavala et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Marchlewska et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This inflated self-image makes individuals more receptive to leaders who claim they can restore the group's status and act as its sole defenders.

As a result, national narcissism is consistently linked to support for populist, anti-democratic, or authoritarian leaders who promise simple solutions to complex problems (Golec de Zavala & Keenan, 2021).
text.formatted: As a result, national narcissism is consistently linked to support for populist, anti-democratic, or authoritarian leaders who promise simple solutions to complex problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Golec de Zavala & Keenan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, individuals high in national narcissism often see democratic processes (with their emphasis on debate, disagreement, compromise, and gradual change) as ineffective and, more importantly, as threatening to their group's fragile self-image (Golec de Zavala & Keenan, 2021).
text.formatted: In other words, individuals high in national narcissism often see democratic processes (with their emphasis on debate, disagreement, compromise, and gradual change) as ineffective and, more importantly, as threatening to their group's fragile self-image (Golec de <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Zavala & Keenan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This defensiveness extends to intolerance toward groups perceived as challenging the ingroup's narrative or status, such as minorities or rival political parties (e.g., Golec de Zavala et al., 2009 , 2016).
text.formatted: This defensiveness extends to intolerance toward groups perceived as challenging the ingroup's narrative or status, such as minorities or rival political parties (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Golec de Zavala et al., 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Because these outgroups are viewed as critics or potential threats to the ingroup's perceived superiority, collective narcissists tend to avoid the dialogue and negotiation that are central to pluralistic societies, thereby undermining their support for democratic norms.
Low democratic support among national narcissists should be particularly acute when evaluating the functioning of democracy within their own country.

This is, in part, because democratic systems, with their emphasis on compromise, pluralism, and the accommodation of diverse interests, are inherently ill-equipped to satisfy the profound and often insatiable psychological needs that fuel collective narcissism -such as the need for constant external validation of the ingroup's superiority and unquestioned special status (Golec de Zavala et al., 2009).
text.formatted: This is, in part, because democratic systems, with their emphasis on compromise, pluralism, and the accommodation of diverse interests, are inherently ill-equipped to satisfy the profound and often insatiable psychological needs that fuel collective narcissism -such as the need for constant external validation of the ingroup's superiority and unquestioned special status <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Golec de Zavala et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: When their nation's democracy fails to deliver on these unrealistic demands, collective narcissists are likely to perceive it not merely as underperforming, but as fundamentally flawed.

This perceived inability of their democracy to cater to these deep-seated, identity-protective needs can then lead them to generalize this frustration, resulting in a low evaluation of democracy as a viable or effective governing system overall, further justifying their preference for leaders and systems that promise to fulfill those narcissistic cravings.
The psychological insecurity underpinning national collective narcissism also manifests in a heightened susceptibility to conspiracy beliefs (Biddlestone et al., 2022; Cichocka et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The psychological insecurity underpinning national collective narcissism also manifests in a heightened susceptibility to conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Biddlestone et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cichocka et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These narratives offer a means to protect a threatened and idealized ingroup image by attributing negative events to the actions of malevolent external forces, rather than confronting internal shortcomings (van Prooijen & Douglas, 2018).
text.formatted: These narratives offer a means to protect a threatened and idealized ingroup image by attributing negative events to the actions of malevolent external forces, rather than confronting internal shortcomings <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(van Prooijen & Douglas, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Given that political knowledge is argued to foster psychological security (Sniderman, 1975), which in turn can buffer against national narcissism (Marchlewska et al., 2022 , Michalski et al., 2023a), it is plausible that greater political knowledge may indirectly reduce the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs.
text.formatted: Given that political knowledge is argued to foster psychological security <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sniderman, 1975)</ref>, which in turn can buffer against national narcissism <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Marchlewska et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">, Michalski et al., 2023a)</ref>, it is plausible that greater political knowledge may indirectly reduce the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs.

text.text: This would occur by diminishing the reliance on national narcissism as a compensatory mechanism for underlying insecurities, thereby lessening the need for conspiratorial explanations to maintain a grandiose ingroup view.
Supporting this mechanism, Michalski et al. (2023a) found that greater rules of the game knowledge reduced climate change conspiracy beliefs by mitigating national narcissism.

text.text: In our research, we examine anti-democratic sentiments (i.e., lower support for democracy, endorsement of dictatorship, and conspiracy beliefs) by focusing on knowledge about the rules of the game.
We assume that lower levels of such knowledge will be positively associated with national narcissism, which, in turn, will predict stronger endorsement of anti-democratic sentiments.
The present research has two primary objectives.

First, it aims to investigate the relationships between dimensions of political knowledge and anti-democratic sentiments (i.e., lower support for democracy, dictatorship endorsement, conspiracy beliefs).

This research, following the works of Michalski and colleagues (2023a, 2023b; also see Delli Carpini and Keeter, 1996), distinguishes and incorporates the rules of the game dimension of political knowledge, referring to an understanding of democratic principles and institutional functions and current political knowledge consisting of facts related to recent political events and prominent political actors.

text.text: Furthermore, we include a direct measure of dictatorship endorsement recognizing that dissatisfaction with democracy does not invariably translate to support for authoritarian regimes (Schedler & Sarsfield, 2007; Wuttke et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Furthermore, we include a direct measure of dictatorship endorsement recognizing that dissatisfaction with democracy does not invariably translate to support for authoritarian regimes <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Schedler & Sarsfield, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wuttke et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, this research seeks to investigate the psychological mechanisms underlying these relationships.

We propose that limited rules of the game knowledge may leave individuals without a clear sense of how democracy works, and that without the psychological security such understanding affords, national narcissism may become a more accessible form of compensation for frustrated psychological needs (Cichocka, 2016; Golec de Zavala et al., 2019).
text.formatted: We propose that limited rules of the game knowledge may leave individuals without a clear sense of how democracy works, and that without the psychological security such understanding affords, national narcissism may become a more accessible form of compensation for frustrated psychological needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cichocka, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Golec de Zavala et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Because rules of the game knowledge and national narcissism each appear to predict lower levels of the other over time (Michalski et al., 2023a), we specify this ordering on theoretical grounds rather than as a causal test.
text.formatted: Because rules of the game knowledge and national narcissism each appear to predict lower levels of the other over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Michalski et al., 2023a)</ref>, we specify this ordering on theoretical grounds rather than as a causal test.

text.text: To further elucidate these mechanisms, in Study 2 we incorporate citizens' evaluation of their own country (i.e., Poland) as a democratic state, linking abstract democratic attitudes to evaluations of a specific national political system.

Individuals scoring high on national narcissism should therefore evaluate democracy in their own country less favorably, to the extent that its institutions are perceived as failing to affirm the ingroup's inflated image and this dissatisfaction should in turn extend to support for democracy in general (Marchlewska et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Individuals scoring high on national narcissism should therefore evaluate democracy in their own country less favorably, to the extent that its institutions are perceived as failing to affirm the ingroup's inflated image and this dissatisfaction should in turn extend to support for democracy in general <ref type="bibr">(Marchlewska et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We attribute this evaluation to these unmet needs rather than to informed appraisal of institutional performance alone.

To this end, we conducted two studies with the two facets of political knowledge (i.e., knowledge about the rules of the game vs. current political knowledge) as independent variables and support for democracy, dictatorship endorsement and conspiracy beliefs as dependent variables.
In all studies, we controlled for national identification to observe the unique effects of national narcissism accounting for its overlap with national identification.

In Study 1, we predicted that higher knowledge about the rules of the game (vs. of current events and actors) would be associated with higher support for democracy (H1), lower dictatorship endorsement (H2) and lower conspiracy beliefs (H3).
We further hypothesized that these associations would be explained by lower national narcissism (H1a, H2a, and H3a, respectively).
Study 2 aimed to replicate and extend these findings by proposing a serial indirect effects model.

Specifically, we predicted that higher knowledge about the rules of the game would be associated with lower national narcissism, which in turn would be associated with higher perceptions of the country's system as democratic.
We hypothesized that this indirect pathway will be associated with higher support for democracy (H4), lower endorsement of dictatorship (H5), and lower belief in conspiracies (H6).

text.text: Recruitment employed quota sampling to ensure that the final group reflected national distributions for key demographics, including sex, age, educational attainment, and size of place of residence.
The resulting sample comprised 705 adults (367 women, 338 men; M age = 47.71, SD age = 15.47).

We measured regime preferences (i.e., support for democracy and dictatorship endorsement) and conspiracy beliefs as dependent variables, two types of political knowledge as independent variables and national narcissism and national identification as mediators.
Unless otherwise noted, all questions employed a 1 (I strongly disagree) to 5 (I strongly agree) response scale 1.

To our knowledge, no previous studies investigated the relationships between discussed two types of political knowledge, national identity and anti-democratic sentiments hence reliable indirect effect sizes from comparable research were unavailable.
Therefore, we were unable to conduct a priori power analyses and the sample size was determined based on economic criteria.
We evaluated statistical power using Monte Carlo simulations based on parameter estimates obtained in Study 1 (5,000 replications) with pwrSEM (Wang & Rhemtulla, 2021).

Taken together, these results indicate that the two dimensions are highly correlated and that the evidence does not decisively establish their empirical distinctness, consistent with prior observations that dimensions of political knowledge tend to be strongly correlated (Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996).

text.text: A high correlation, however, need not imply theoretical redundancy: general dispositions toward acquiring knowledge coexist with substantial differentiation across content domains (Ackerman, 1996), suggesting that the shared variance of the two dimensions reflects a general propensity to be knowledgeable, while what distinguishes them lies in their unique variance.

text.text: Our analyses therefore focus on the unique variance of each dimension, where contentspecific relations should be more clearly located.
We treat the two-dimensional distinction as theoretically motivated and interpret the dimension-specific findings with appropriate caution.

Study 1 aimed to examine how knowledge about the rules of the game relates to antidemocratic sentiments.
The findings supported our predictions.

In line with our central hypothesis, knowledge about the rules of the game was indirectly associated with support for democracy (H1), dictatorship endorsement (H2), and conspiracy beliefs (H3), with these indirect associations operating through lower national narcissism (H1a, H2a, and H3a respectively).

These results highlight that understanding democratic principles, more so than awareness of current events, is linked to pro-democratic orientations, largely through its association with lower national narcissism.
At the same time, an opposite pattern emerged for current political knowledge when controlling for knowledge about the rules of the game.
Greater awareness of current political events and political actors net of knowledge about democratic principles was associated with higher national narcissism.

In turn, current political knowledge was indirectly associated with lower support for democracy and with higher dictatorship endorsement and conspiracy beliefs through its association with higher national narcissism.

This pattern suggests that the relationship between political knowledge and anti-democratic attitudes may depend not only on how much individuals know, but also on the type of political knowledge they possess.
In Study 2, we aimed to replicate these findings and, additionally, extended our model by testing a serial indirect effects pathway.
Specifically, we investigated whether perceptions of the country's political system as democratic would function as a key link between national narcissism and its negative outcomes.

We predicted that higher national narcissism would be associated with perception of Poland as less democratic (i.e., government is less receptive to citizens' opinions, civil rights are not respected etc.) given its links with limited understanding of democratic norms and outcomes misaligned with national narcissists' desires (i.e., protection of inflated group image).
This negative perception, in turn, was expected to be associated with less democratic regime preferences and greater endorsement of conspiracy beliefs.
For Study 2, data were collected via a different online research panel, Pollster, a platform with prior experience in academic research (e.g., Michalski et al., 2023a).

Study 2 aimed to replicate and extend the findings of Study 1.

A key extension was the introduction of a new variable: the perception of Poland as a democratic state, which captures citizens' subjective assessment of how well their country's political system adheres to democratic principles.

The results largely replicated the core findings from Study 1: knowledge about the rules of the game was again associated with more favorable democratic attitudes via lower national narcissism which confirmed our hypotheses.

Consistent with our primary hypotheses and Study 1, knowledge about the rules of the game was negatively associated with national narcissism, which in turn was indirectly associated with higher support for democracy, lower dictatorship endorsement, and lower conspiracy beliefs.

Furthermore, serial indirect effects analyses indicated that knowledge about the rules of the game was associated with all three dependent variables sequentially through its association with national narcissism and subsequently through its association with the perception of Poland as a democratic state.
This suggests that national narcissists, fueled by a lack of knowledge about the rules of the game, report lower evaluations of their own country's democratic system.
This is likely because it is unable to fulfill their extremely high expectations related to idealized and grandiose ingroup image.
Furthermore, results of serial indirect effects analyses provided support for the hypothesized theoretical model.

Taken together, these findings suggest that lower levels of this knowledge are associated with stronger narcissistic identity, which is in turn linked to more negative evaluations of the democratic functioning of one's own country, and ultimately to greater rejection of democracy as a system and stronger endorsement of conspiracy beliefs.

Study 2 also replicated findings related to negative associations of current political knowledge, net of knowledge about the rules of the game, with anti-democratic sentiments via national narcissism.
However, results also indicated a reversed, yet weaker, relationships with the dependent variables via national identification.

Taken together, these dual pathways suggest that current political knowledge is neither straightforwardly beneficial nor harmful for democratic attitudes, but its function depends on the psychological channel through which it operates.

When current political awareness heightens national narcissism, it may serve as a vehicle for antidemocratic sentiment, particularly when the political discourse is dominated by conflict or threatframing narratives.

Yet its weaker, positive indirect association via national identification suggests a civic potential: staying informed may also reinforce a sense of shared belonging that is potentially beneficial for democracy.
The contemporary erosion of democratic norms has spurred urgent questions about the psychological factors that lead citizens to turn away from democracy.
The present research sought to address this issue by exploring the protective role of political knowledge against anti-democratic sentiments.
We proposed that this relationship is not straightforward but is instead driven by a specific psychological mechanism: the mitigation of national narcissism.

We found that knowledge about the rules of the game, but not current political knowledge, had the potential to reduce psychological defensiveness in the form of national narcissism, a compensatory mechanism for coping with psychological shortcomings (Cichocka et al., 2018; Cichocka & Cisłak, 2020; Golec de Zavala et al., 2019; Marchlewska et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We found that knowledge about the rules of the game, but not current political knowledge, had the potential to reduce psychological defensiveness in the form of national narcissism, a compensatory mechanism for coping with psychological shortcomings <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cichocka et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cichocka & Cisłak, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Golec de Zavala et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Marchlewska et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Across two studies conducted in Poland, our findings consistently supported this theoretical model.
We demonstrated that knowledge about the rules of the game, rather than mere awareness of current political events, was negatively related to anti-democratic sentiments.

Study 1 established that this type of knowledge was associated with lower national narcissism, which in turn predicted greater support for democracy, lower endorsement of dictatorship and lower conspiracy beliefs.
Study 2 replicated these core findings and added a contextual-related variable (i.e., evaluation of political system in democratic terms).

The results showed that individuals with greater rules of the game knowledge were less prone to identify with their nation in narcissistic fashion, and therefore more likely to perceive their own country's political system as democratic, which was associated with weaker anti-democratic sentiments.

Together, these studies suggest that it is the deep, structural knowledge of democratic processes (i.e., what are democratic norms and principles and why they are crucial for this type of government) that serves as a crucial psychological buffer, protecting citizens from the allure of national narcissism and its anti-democratic consequences.
Relations between political knowledge and anti-democratic sentiments are, however, more nuanced.
Specifically, current political knowledge showed the opposite relationship with national narcissism than knowledge about the rules of the game after controlling for their shared variance.

Statistically, this reversal reflects a suppression effect -although both dimensions were negatively correlated with national narcissism at the zero-order level, the unique component of current political knowledge was positively associated with it.

This pattern replicated across both studies with coefficients of comparable magnitude (β = .38 and β = .31), and collinearity diagnostics were unproblematic in both (see footnotes 5 and 11), which suggests a stable estimate rather than one destabilized by the high correlation between the two dimensions.
It indicates that the shared and unique portions of current political knowledge relate to national narcissism in opposite ways.

One possible interpretation of the opposing associations is that national narcissism may be linked not to political awareness per se, but to a specific configuration of political knowledge: relatively high awareness of current political events combined with limited understanding of democratic institutions.

In such cases, individuals may be attentive to political conflict and perceived threats while lacking the institutional framework needed to interpret these dynamics as normal features of democratic systems.
This imbalance may foster perceptions of instability or threat, which align with the defensive worldview characteristic of national narcissism (Cichocka, 2016; Cichocka et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This imbalance may foster perceptions of instability or threat, which align with the defensive worldview characteristic of national narcissism <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cichocka, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cichocka et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern resonates with Norris's (2011) notion of the "critical citizen" -someone highly attentive to political affairs yet dissatisfied with how democratic institutions perform.
text.formatted: This pattern resonates with <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Norris's (2011)</ref> notion of the "critical citizen" -someone highly attentive to political affairs yet dissatisfied with how democratic institutions perform.

text.text: While Norris (2011) originally framed such dissatisfaction as potentially constructive for democracy, our findings suggest a more troubling possibility: when political attentiveness is not grounded in an understanding of democratic principles, it may reinforce grievance rather than engagement.

Without a grasp of why democratic systems are inherently slow, contested, and compromise-driven, politically aware individuals may read the normal friction of democratic governance as evidence of failure or elite manipulation -narratives that national narcissism readily amplifies.

This also has broader implications for civic education efforts: increasing political awareness without simultaneously deepening citizens' understanding of democratic norms and institutions may not only fail to protect against anti-democratic sentiments, but could, under certain conditions, contribute to them.
This is not to say, however, that current political knowledge is without democratic value.

A deep understanding of democratic principles may anchor citizens' commitment to the system, while vigilant monitoring of the political landscape is essential for critically evaluating political actors and identifying those who may pose a threat to citizens' self-interests.

Indeed, citizens with up-to-date political knowledge are better equipped to assess how well political elites represent their preferences and interests -a core component of democratic legitimacy (Dalton, 2018).
text.formatted: Indeed, citizens with up-to-date political knowledge are better equipped to assess how well political elites represent their preferences and interests -a core component of democratic legitimacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dalton, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: While this type of knowledge helps translate individual interests into political choices and actions, it is knowledge about the rules of the game that orients those choices within a democratic frameworkensuring that personal goals are pursued in ways that respect pluralism, the rule of law, and institutional checks and balances.
This distinction helps clarify why, in our findings, it was knowledge about the rules of the game, not current political knowledge, that consistently buffered against anti-democratic sentiments.
The interpretation of these divergent relations, however, must be considered in light of the strong correlation between the two dimensions.
Knowledge across broad domains tends to be positively correlated, as its acquisition draws on shared antecedents such as general cognitive ability (Ackerman, 1996).
text.formatted: Knowledge across broad domains tends to be positively correlated, as its acquisition draws on shared antecedents such as general cognitive ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ackerman, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Political knowledge is no different in this respect.

As a form of knowledge, its dimensions rest on the same general foundations, while also drawing on more specific antecedents such as political interest and opportunities to acquire political information (Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996).
text.formatted: As a form of knowledge, its dimensions rest on the same general foundations, while also drawing on more specific antecedents such as political interest and opportunities to acquire political information <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Delli Carpini & Keeter, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The variance shared by the two types of political knowledge therefore largely reflects a general tendency to be politically knowledgeable, rather than what is distinctive about either type.

For this reason, our analyses focus on the unique variance of each dimension, which, we argue, better captures the content specific to a given type of knowledge and its distinct relations with other variables.
This focus on unique variance is what allows the opposing associations of the two dimensions with national narcissism to surface.
Their divergence, in turn, indicates that the two forms of political knowledge occupy different regions of the nomological network (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955).
text.formatted: Their divergence, in turn, indicates that the two forms of political knowledge occupy different regions of the nomological network <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cronbach & Meehl, 1955)</ref>.

text.text: It also has a broader implication, because treating political knowledge as a unidimensional construct may obscure the distinct, and sometimes opposing, relations that its components bear to external variables -in our case, national narcissism.
This relationship is further complicated considering the nature of national narcissism.

Our model proposes that rules of the game knowledge fosters psychological security (Sniderman, 1975), thereby diminishing the need for the defensive compensation that defines national narcissism (Cichocka, 2016).
text.formatted: Our model proposes that rules of the game knowledge fosters psychological security <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sniderman, 1975)</ref>, thereby diminishing the need for the defensive compensation that defines national narcissism <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cichocka, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, the relationship may be bidirectional, creating a self-reinforcing cycle.

In fact, studies by Michalski and colleagues (2023a) found not only that knowledge about the rules of the game may attenuate national narcissism, but also that individuals high in national narcissism were less likely to acquire knowledge about the rules of the game over time.
text.formatted: In fact, studies by <ref type="bibr">Michalski and colleagues (2023a)</ref> found not only that knowledge about the rules of the game may attenuate national narcissism, but also that individuals high in national narcissism were less likely to acquire knowledge about the rules of the game over time.

text.text: This suggests that national narcissism not only stems from a knowledge deficit but also actively obstructs the learning process, making it difficult to reach narcissistic individuals with civic education.

Adding to this complexity, research by Górska and colleagues (2023) showed that national narcissism and antidemocratic sentiments (i.e., conspiracy beliefs and right-wing authoritarianism) also mutually reinforce each other over time.
text.formatted: Adding to this complexity, research by <ref type="bibr">Górska and colleagues (2023)</ref> showed that national narcissism and antidemocratic sentiments (i.e., conspiracy beliefs and right-wing authoritarianism) also mutually reinforce each other over time.

text.text: The results of our studies, thus, emphasize the role of knowledge about the rules of the game as a potential antidote capable of interrupting this self-perpetuating, democracy-eroding cycle.
A key challenge for future research is to explore how effective civic education should be designed to circumvent the defensive mechanisms that prevent learning among national narcissists.

Furthermore, our research extends the theoretical understanding of how national narcissism translates into anti-democratic sentiment by introducing a key intervening construct: the perception of one's own country as a high-functioning democracy.
Results of Study 2 indicated that lack of knowledge about the rules of the game was related to higher national narcissism and in turn predicted a more negative evaluation of Poland's democracy.
This dissatisfaction is not arbitrary.

It stems from the inherent inability of a pluralistic, compromise-based democratic system to provide what national narcissists psychologically crave: constant external validation of the nation's greatness and the soothing of their deep-seated insecurities (Cichocka et al., 2018; Golec de Zavala & Keenan, 2021).
text.formatted: It stems from the inherent inability of a pluralistic, compromise-based democratic system to provide what national narcissists psychologically crave: constant external validation of the nation's greatness and the soothing of their deep-seated insecurities <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cichocka et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Golec de Zavala & Keenan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: By devaluing their own nation's democratic processes as flawed and incapable of delivering this recognition, individuals high in national narcissism may more easily justify their turn towards authoritarian alternatives that promise to restore the nation's "true" greatness.
This finding illustrates why citizens who lack knowledge about the rules of the game and adopt a narcissistic identity find anti-democratic sentiments so appealing.
The present research has several limitations that offer valuable directions for future investigation.
First, the cross-sectional nature of our data precludes causal claims.

For instance, an experimental design could test whether an intervention aimed at increasing knowledge about the rules of the game leads to a subsequent decrease in national narcissism and anti-democratic attitudes.
A further limitation concerns the dimensionality of political knowledge.

The two facets were strongly correlated, and the discriminant validity evidence was mixed, supportive in Study 2 but only marginal in Study 1, so we cannot claim with certainty that they are fully separable constructs.

Importantly, this does not undermine our finding that the unique parts of the two dimensions relate to national narcissism in different, and even opposite, ways -this pattern was robust and replicated across studies.
What remains less certain is how these unique parts should be interpreted.

Because the two dimensions overlap so heavily, the labeling of their unique components rests on the theoretical interpretation we develop in this paper, rather than on the discriminant validity evidence alone.

Related to this, we do not claim that two dimensions exhaust the construct of political knowledge, which is regarded as multifaceted and unlikely to be fully captured by a limited set of indicators (Barabas et al., 2014; Johann, 2012).

text.text: Building on the work of Barabas et al. (2014), we focused on two dimensions: a structural one, concerning the relatively stable rules and institutions that define how the political system works, and a temporal one, concerning the events and actors that occupy that system at a given moment.

(2014)</ref>, we focused on two dimensions: a structural one, concerning the relatively stable rules and institutions that define how the political system works, and a temporal one, concerning the events and actors that occupy that system at a given moment.

text.text: The role of the past, however, was omitted.

Knowledge of political history, particularly of systemic transformations such as Poland's transition from authoritarian rule to democracy, provides an interpretive lens for evaluating present political developments and may be no less consequential for democratic attitudes than knowledge about the rules of the game.

It is also a theoretically interesting case, since such knowledge could relate to national narcissism in either direction by supporting an appreciation of how democratic institutions have been won and lost, or instead furnishing narratives of national grievance and lost greatness (see e.g., Główczewski et al., 2022; Klar & Bilewicz, 2017).
text.formatted: It is also a theoretically interesting case, since such knowledge could relate to national narcissism in either direction by supporting an appreciation of how democratic institutions have been won and lost, or instead furnishing narratives of national grievance and lost greatness (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Główczewski et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Klar & Bilewicz, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Clarifying how additional dimensions such as this one fit within the structure of political knowledge, and how each relates to defensive national identity, is an important task for future work.
While our findings provide support for the proposed psychological mechanisms, some elements of our model were inferred rather than directly measured.

We theorized knowledge about the rules of the game enhances psychological security (in contrast to current political knowledge), which in turn reduces national narcissism, but we did not include a direct measure of individuallevel psychological security in our studies.
Future research should explicitly measure this construct to provide more direct evidence for its mediating role.
Another limitation was related to the measurement of conspiracy beliefs.
We used a general measure to capture overall susceptibility to conspiracy thinking (Brotherton et al., 2013), in line with our aim to treat it as a broader indicator of anti-democratic sentiment.
text.formatted: We used a general measure to capture overall susceptibility to conspiracy thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brotherton et al., 2013)</ref>, in line with our aim to treat it as a broader indicator of anti-democratic sentiment.

text.text: However, recent work suggests that different types of conspiracy beliefs may serve distinct functions (Nera, 2024; Sutton et al., 2024), especially in the context of research on collective narcissism (e.g., Karakula et al., 2025 Karakula et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: However, recent work suggests that different types of conspiracy beliefs may serve distinct functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Nera, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sutton et al., 2024)</ref>, especially in the context of research on collective narcissism (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Karakula et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Karakula et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Our measure included non-political content, which did not allow us to distinguish between such forms.
Future research should use more specific measures aligned with the research context.

Finally, our studies were conducted exclusively in Poland which limits the generalizability of our findings to other political environments, such as countries with longer democratic traditions (e.g., the United States or the United Kingdom).

Cross-cultural replications are essential to establish the broader validity of our model and to understand how the interplay between political knowledge, national narcissism, and pro-democratic sentiments varies across different societal contexts.

Overall, our studies extend previous research by pointing to psychological mechanisms that may help account for why individuals with greater knowledge about the rules of the game tend to be less likely to endorse anti-democratic sentiments.

Our findings suggest that a deeper understanding of democratic principles may be linked to lower levels of national narcissism, which in turn appears to relate to more favorable evaluations of democracy in one's own country and stronger democratic attitudes.
However, important questions remain open.
At what stage of life can such educational interventions be most effective?
In what contexts can these methods of democratic education be implemented?
Can high-quality civic education meaningfully counteract the appeal of antidemocratic beliefs?
These questions call for further empirical investigation.

text.text: Consistent with our hypotheses and the findings from Study 1, the analyses revealed several significant indirect effects.

First, knowledge about the rules of the game showed significant indirect associations with support for democracy (IE = 0.22, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.13, 0.33], p < .001), dictatorship endorsement (IE = -0.22, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.31, -0.14], p < .001), and conspiracy beliefs (IE = -0.25, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.37, -0.17], p < .001), operating through its association with lower national narcissism.
text.formatted: First, knowledge about the rules of the game showed significant indirect associations with support for democracy (IE = 0.22, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.13, 0.33], p < .001), dictatorship endorsement (IE = -0.22, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.31, -0.14], p < .001), and conspiracy beliefs (IE = -0.25, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.37, -0.17], p < .001), operating through its association with lower national narcissism.

text.text: Next, we tested the hypothesized serial indirect effects, where knowledge about the rules of the game was associated with the dependent variables first through its association with lower national narcissism and then through its association with higher perception of Poland as a democratic state.
All three tested serial indirect effects were significant.

Specifically, the serial indirect association with support for democracy was significant (IE = 0.11, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [0.07, 0.17], p < .001), as was the serial indirect association with dictatorship endorsement (IE = -0.04, SE = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.07, -0.01], p < .01) and with conspiracy beliefs (IE = -0.17, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.11], p < .001).
text.formatted: Specifically, the serial indirect association with support for democracy was significant (IE = 0.11, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [0.07, 0.17], p < .001), as was the serial indirect association with dictatorship endorsement (IE = -0.04, SE = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.07, -0.01], p < .01) and with conspiracy beliefs (IE = -0.17, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.11], p < .001).

text.text: Additionally, we tested whether current political knowledge, controlled for knowledge about the rules of the game, was associated with anti-democratic sentiments through its association with higher national narcissism.

Results showed significant indirect effects: higher current political knowledge was associated with lower support for democracy (IE = -0.12, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.21, -0.06], p < .001), higher dictatorship endorsement (IE = 0.12, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.07, 0.19], p < .001), and higher conspiracy beliefs (IE = 0.14, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.08, 0.23], p < .001), operating through its association with higher national narcissism.

text.text: Interestingly, we also observed a reversed pattern regarding the associations of current political knowledge operating through national identification.

Specifically, current political knowledge showed positive indirect associations with support for democracy (IE = 0.07, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.03, 0.13], p < .01), and negative indirect associations with dictatorship endorsement (IE = -0.06, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.10, -0.02], p < .01) and conspiracy beliefs (IE = -0.05, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.09, -0.01], p < .05), operating through its association with higher national identification.
